analysis.one_liner: Lets energy regulators order natural gas companies to refund overcharges to consumers, with interest.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate Energy Committee until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which oversees interstate natural gas pipelines, order gas companies to refund customers money collected through rates found unjust or unreasonable. It would require refunds with interest, put the burden of proof on the gas company to show a rate change is fair, and set deadlines for decisions. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that buy natural gas delivered through interstate pipelines. Under current law, FERC can generally order refunds only from the date it acts on a complaint; this bill would allow refunds covering the period during the review, up to 150 days back, so customers recoup overcharges instead of eating them.

how_it_helps.text: Requires natural gas companies to pay refunds with interest to consumers for charges FERC finds unjust, unreasonable, or discriminatory.
Puts the burden of proof on the natural gas company to show a changed rate is just and reasonable, rather than making consumers prove it is not.
Requires FERC to establish a refund effective date no later than 150 days after a complaint or notice is filed, limiting how long companies can keep collected overcharges.

analysis.who_pays: Interstate natural gas pipeline companies, which could be ordered to return collected revenue with interest if FERC finds their rates excessive. Those costs could partly flow through to future rates or shareholder returns.

drawbacks.text: Pipeline companies and some policymakers argue that mandatory refunds and a shifted burden of proof raise companies' cost of capital and could increase future rates or slow pipeline investment; the bill itself directs FERC to study these effects three to four years after enactment.

The bill sets decision deadlines only as a reporting requirement: if FERC misses its 180-day window it must merely explain why and estimate a decision date, not actually decide in time, so delays for consumers could persist.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the direct benefit is real but bounded: refunds on specific overcharges found unjust, plus interest, during a defined window. The main costs fall on gas companies, though higher perceived financial risk could show up in future rates, which is why the bill mandates a study of exactly that. No counterweighing consumer cost is identified in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2024 and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, with one Republican cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day; no further action was ever taken.
The committee held no hearing, marked up no text, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas pipeline companies came out ahead: they face no new refund obligations, keep any revenue collected through rates that were never challenged or were challenged too late, and the status quo limiting consumer refunds remains intact. Consumers who would have received refunds did not.

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and argued in its title and text for making pipelines refund overcharges to consumers.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican joined the Democratic sponsor, giving it a two-senator start, but neither party's leadership moved it; no votes were ever taken to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would require them to refund, with interest, rates FERC finds unjust or unreasonable, and would make them prove rate changes are fair rather than leaving that burden on consumers. Their financial interest in keeping collected revenue runs against the consumers the refunds would go to.

industries.industry: Natural gas utilities and ratepayer-funded shareholders
industries.note: Utilities delivering gas to retail customers could benefit from refunds passed through, but would also face regulatory scrutiny and potential repayment if their own upstream rates are challenged. The net effect depends on how costs flow through rates.
